extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and writers studying Kurt Vonnegut, satire, or comic/satirical fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria drawn from a Kurt Vonnegut biography describing his style, themes, and techniques—useful for analyzing his work or emulating his approach to comic/socially critical fiction. Focuses on voice, prose economy, thematic emphases, and formal experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write like a human being
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted guidance from Vonnegut: 'Write like a human being. Write like a writer.' (from Pity the Reader: On Writing with Style)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat prose as conversation with a human reader—avoid artificial voice or obscurantism; prioritize naturalness and readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct narrative voice combining energy, despair, satire and warmth
rubrics_metrics.description: Vonnegut's voice is described as 'manic depressive' with 'an incredible amount of energy married to a very deep and dark sense of despair... frequently over-the-top, and scathingly satirical, but it never strays too far from pathos—from an immense sympathy for society's vulnerable, oppressed and powerless. But, then, it also contains a huge allotment of warmth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a voice that balances high-energy satire with genuine sympathy and warmth; keep the narrator present and engaging ('right there in the foreground—direct, involving and extremely idiosyncratic'). Avoid purely ironic detachment that removes empathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise, simple, conversational prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Michael D. Sharp: Vonnegut's linguistic style is 'straightforward, his sentences concise, his language simple, his paragraphs brief, and his ordinary tone conversational.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor clarity: short sentences, plain diction, brief paragraphs, and an ordinary conversational tone. Make complex subjects intelligible to a broad audience by stripping unnecessary ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a youthful or childlike narrative perspective when useful
rubrics_metrics.description: Vonnegut modelled his style after Thoreau, 'who wrote as if from the perspective of a child, allowing Thoreau's works to be widely comprehensible.' Using a youthful narrative voice allowed Vonnegut 'to deliver concepts in a modest and straightforward way.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider a seemingly naive, childlike vantage to render philosophical or social ideas more accessible and rhetorically disarming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use autobiographical material and self-reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Vonnegut's compositions include 'distinct references to his own life, notably in Slaughterhouse-Five and Slapstick.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intersperse fictional work with autobiographical detail or personal perspective to ground satire and lend authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize ideas and convincing communication
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Vonnegut believed that ideas and the convincing communication of those ideas to the reader were vital to literary art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate success by how clearly and persuasively the central idea is communicated; style should serve concept and argument rather than obscure it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use humor as a vehicle to teach and reveal bitter truths
rubrics_metrics.description: Tally & Kunze: Vonnegut used 'comic parables' to teach the reader absurd, bitter or hopeless truths, with his grim witticisms serving to make the reader laugh rather than cry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for humor that illuminates social or moral realities; laughter should open understanding rather than merely entertain. Use comic framing to deliver serious critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist narrow genre labeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Vonnegut 'resented being called a black humorist, feeling that, as with many literary labels, it allowed readers to disregard aspects of a writer's work that did not fit the label.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid rigid adherence to a single genre label; be willing to blend satire, science fiction, metafiction, and realist elements as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ science‑fiction and satirical tropes strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: Vonnegut's works 'have been labeled science fiction, satire and postmodern' and 'do contain common tropes in those genres... imagines alien societies and civilizations... emphasizes or exaggerates absurdities and idiosyncrasies.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use genre conventions (aliens, imagined societies, speculative devices) to amplify satire and to create distance for critique, but do so with purpose rather than as mere ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fragmentation and metafiction to question representation of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics note Vonnegut uses 'metafictional, Janus-headed outlook' and techniques like 'unreliable, first-person narration, and narrative fragmentation' to represent and doubt historical events and truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply postmodern techniques (fragmentation, metafictional commentary, unreliable narrators) to problematize claims of objective truth and call attention to narrative construction—but ensure these techniques serve thematic aims (e.g., war, trauma), not gimmickry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus thematic attention on the peril of imposing subjective 'truths'
rubrics_metrics.description: Although Vonnegut uses fragmentation and metafiction, 'he more distinctly focuses on the peril of individuals who find subjective truths, mistake them for objective truths, and proceed to impose these truths on other people.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use satire to expose the danger of absolutist belief systems and the harm of imposing personal certainties on others; structural choices should highlight that peril.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment with the novel's form to map fragmented social experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Tally: Vonnegut's '14 novels... together are nevertheless experiments in the same overall project... Experimenting with the form of the American novel itself... attempt to apprehend and depict the fragmented, unstable, and distressing bizarreries of postmodern American experience.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to alter conventional narrative structures (nonlinear timelines, mixed genres, episodic forms) to reflect social fragmentation. The experimentation should be purposeful in service of theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use religion and religious rhetoric as thematic and rhetorical tools
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Religion features frequently in Vonnegut's work... he admired Jesus's Sermon on the Mount' and incorporated religious motifs (e.g., invented faiths like Bokononism) as plot devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage religious language, institutions, and parody of faiths to explore moral questions, hypocrisy, consolation, and communal belonging—treat religion both as critique and as source of ethical insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulate anti‑war sentiment without glamorizing conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Vonnegut was 'a pacifist' and described Slaughterhouse-Five as antiwar; he 'wanted to write war-focused works without glamorizing war itself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict war's horrors and human cost candidly; use irony and satire to undercut martial glamor and to foreground civilian suffering and moral consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique technological progress and its human costs
rubrics_metrics.description: A recurring theme: 'the negative effects of the progress of technology... Loss of jobs due to machine innovation, and thus loss of meaning or purpose in life, is a key plot point' (e.g., Player Piano).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use speculative devices and plot consequences to show how technological 'progress' can erode purpose, imagination, and communal life; dramatize human impacts rather than technical details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address economic inequality and social Darwinism
rubrics_metrics.description: Vonnegut 'points out that, left unchecked, capitalism will erode the democratic foundations...' and often treats wealth and its unequal distribution as central social themes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Center critiques of capitalism and inherited wealth in character situations and plot mechanics; show social consequences rather than relying on didactic polemic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explore ethical obligations in science
rubrics_metrics.description: Science and the ethical obligations of scientists are a common theme; Vonnegut described the 'virtuous scientist' as 'one who declines to work on weapons.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In narratives involving scientists or inventions, foreground moral responsibility and potential misuse; dramatize ethical dilemmas rather than neutral technocratic exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage with existential questions—free will, purpose, despair
rubrics_metrics.description: Vonnegut confronts 'free will' (characters lacking choice) and recurring concerns about loss of purpose in life and suicide; his works ask 'What is the point of life?'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use character arcs and speculative conceits to interrogate agency, meaning, and human suffering; balance bleak insights with humane concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use recurring motifs and invented cosmologies (e.g., Tralfamadore) to satirize and escape
rubrics_metrics.description: Tralfamadore is a recurring motif used as 'an outlet for escapism' and to provide vantage points for criticizing humanity; its inhabitants often display low esteem of humanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create recurring fictional devices (planets, mythologies, religions) that allow sustained thematic interrogation across works and provide satirical distance for social critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foster intimacy and inclusiveness with the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading Vonnegut 'feels more like being spoken to by a very close friend... There's an inclusiveness to his writing that draws you in.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt rhetorical strategies (direct address, conversational tone, confiding narrator) that make readers feel included and implicated rather than lectured.
